title: Balance: Two Codes for Every Head Movement

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Why can severe loss of both vestibular organs make vision blur during walking?
cards.back: Reduced vestibular input weakens the vestibulo-ocular reflex, so the eyes compensate less effectively for head rotation and the image moves on the retina.
cards.quote: this reflex turns the eyes against head rotation to hold the image still.

cards.front: What movements do the semicircular canals and otolith organs sense?
cards.back: Canals sense head rotation; otolith organs sense linear acceleration and tilt.
cards.quote: the canals, which sense rotation and over ordinary movements report roughly the head's rotational velocity, the otoliths, which sense linear acceleration and tilt

cards.front: A vestibular afferent's {{c1::gain}} is the change in firing rate for a given motion.
cards.quote: a fibre's gain is how much its rate changes for a given motion.
cards.section: Two channels for one head movement

cards.front: How does firing at a high resting rate let a vestibular afferent signal motion in either direction?
cards.back: Motion can increase or decrease firing relative to the resting rate, allowing changes in both directions.
cards.quote: so each can signal motion in either direction by speeding up or slowing down.
cards.section: Two channels for one head movement

cards.front: What spike-train measurement distinguishes regular from irregular vestibular afferents at rest?
cards.back: The coefficient of variation (CV) of interspike intervals: low for regular afferents, high for irregular afferents. These are ends of a continuum.
cards.quote: Regularity at rest is measured by the coefficient of variation (CV) of the intervals between spikes
cards.section: Two channels for one head movement

cards.front: How do regular and irregular canal afferents differ in the information they carry?
cards.back: Regular afferents mainly encode angular velocity in firing rate. Irregular afferents have higher gain and emphasize rapid changes through precise spike timing.
cards.quote: Most of a regular canal fibre's information is in its rate.
cards.section: The signature: two spike trains

cards.front: A head rotation continues at steady speed, while a separate trial holds the head tilted relative to gravity. What happens to sustained canal versus regular otolith signalling, and why?
cards.back: The canal signal fades; the regular otolith signal persists during the held tilt because gravity continues to act along its preferred direction.
cards.quote: so regular otolith fibres keep reporting it for as long as it lasts.
cards.section: The signature: two spike trains

cards.front: Why can a low-gain regular canal afferent detect smaller slow rotations than a high-gain irregular afferent?
cards.back: In the lesson’s toy spike-count decoder, threshold = noise/gain. Regular afferents can have sufficiently less rate noise to outweigh their lower gain.
cards.quote: The quiet, low-gain fibre wins, because its noise is far smaller and its gain only three times smaller.
cards.section: A paradox: lower gain, better detection

cards.front: In a toy spike-count decoder, both fibres fire at 100 spikes/s. Regular: CV = 0.05, gain = 0.5 (spikes/s)/(degree/s). Irregular: CV = 0.5, gain = 1.5 in the same units. Using noise = √(CV² × rate/time), estimate noise/gain thresholds over 1 s.
cards.back: Regular noise = √(0.05² × 100/1) = 0.5 spikes/s; threshold = 0.5/0.5 = 1 degree/s. Irregular noise = √(0.5² × 100/1) = 5 spikes/s; threshold = 5/1.5 ≈ 3.3 degrees/s. These are rough long-window estimates.
cards.quote: A rough rule for long windows puts the rate's standard deviation at √(CV² × rate / time).
cards.section: A paradox: lower gain, better detection

cards.front: A toy vestibular decoder must shorten its spike-count window to report rapid changes. Why might adding a spike-timing readout help, even if the regular fibre remains the better rate-based detector?
cards.back: Rapid rate estimates become less reliable in short windows. Combining that rule with the irregular channel’s precise timing suggests a timing readout could add rapid-motion information. The rate-threshold ranking alone cannot rank all decoding strategies.
cards.quote: In this toy, a fast local rate estimate is much less reliable, which leaves room for the irregular fibre's other strength
cards.section: A paradox: lower gain, better detection

cards.front: An afferent has uneven resting spike intervals. How would replaying an identical rapid head-motion waveform distinguish stimulus-locked timing from random spike noise?
cards.back: Compare spike times across repeated presentations. Spikes recurring near the same stimulus moments support stimulus-locked timing; pure noise would not show that reproducibility.
cards.quote: A fibre whose spikes are locked to the motion fires at nearly the same moments on every repeat
cards.section: Irregular at rest, precise when it matters

cards.front: What are the shape and afferent ending of a mammalian type I vestibular hair cell?
cards.back: It is flask-shaped, with a cup-shaped calyx almost completely enclosing its basolateral membrane.
cards.quote: A type I cell is flask-shaped, and its afferent ending, a cup-shaped calyx, almost completely encloses the basolateral membrane.
cards.section: Where each channel comes from

cards.front: What are the shape and afferent endings of a mammalian type II vestibular hair cell?
cards.back: It is cylindrical and receives several small bouton endings.
cards.quote: A type II cell is cylindrical and receives several small bouton endings.
cards.section: Where each channel comes from

cards.front: What distinguishes calyx-only, bouton-only and dimorphic vestibular afferents?
cards.back: Calyx-only fibres contact type I cells through calyces; bouton-only fibres contact type II cells through boutons; dimorphic fibres carry both kinds of ending.
cards.quote: One afferent can carry more than one kind of ending, which gives three kinds of fibre.
cards.section: Where each channel comes from

cards.front: Where are the main populations of calyx-only, bouton-only and dimorphic vestibular afferents found?
cards.back: Calyx-only fibres mostly occupy the central zone; bouton-only fibres mostly occupy the peripheral zone; dimorphic fibres occur in both.
cards.quote: Each channel has a home in the organ, as a population pattern.
cards.section: Where each channel comes from

cards.front: Why does finding a calyx ending not establish that a vestibular afferent fires irregularly?
cards.back: The anatomy-to-firing map describes populations. Regular fibres can carry calyces, and irregular fibres can have only boutons; the calyx alone does not establish regularity.
cards.quote: regular discharge can come from fibres with calyx endings, irregular discharge from fibres with only boutons
cards.section: Where each channel comes from

cards.front: What is a vestibular-evoked myogenic potential (VEMP), and which afferent pathway does it mainly report?
cards.back: A neck- or eye-muscle reflex response to sound or vibration, mainly reporting irregular otolith afferents from the striola.
cards.quote: Sound and bone-conducted vibration mostly activate irregular otolith afferents from the striola.
cards.section: Where each channel comes from

cards.front: What vesicular signalling mechanism do both vestibular hair-cell types share?
cards.back: Both use calcium-dependent quantal glutamate release at ribbon synapses; each quantum is one vesicle.
cards.quote: Both hair-cell types release glutamate by calcium-dependent quantal release, in packets of one vesicle each, at ribbon synapses
cards.section: A synapse that need not wait for vesicles

cards.front: What defines non-quantal transmission from a vestibular type I hair cell to its calyx?
cards.back: A change in calyx potential without vesicular exocytosis and without gap junctions.
cards.quote: Formally, it is a change in calyx potential without vesicular exocytosis and without gap junctions
cards.section: A synapse that need not wait for vesicles

cards.front: Why could the fast electrical component of type I–calyx non-quantal transmission reduce synaptic delay?
cards.back: It bypasses vesicle fusion, glutamate diffusion and receptor opening. The potassium-accumulation component builds more slowly.
cards.quote: a vesicle has to fuse, glutamate has to cross the cleft, and receptors have to open, and each step adds delay.
cards.section: A synapse that need not wait for vesicles

cards.front: Mature mouse utricle type I cells lacking otoferlin or CaV1.3 still drove calyx action potentials in vitro. What does this support, and what does it leave untested?
cards.back: It supports a functional route that does not require vesicle fusion. Survival of evoked spikes does not establish that transmission remains normal.
cards.quote: The test was whether spikes survive, in vitro, not whether the signal is normal.
cards.section: A synapse that need not wait for vesicles

cards.front: Why can potassium accumulate between a vestibular type I hair cell and its calyx during hair-cell depolarization?
cards.back: The enclosing calyx creates a narrow cleft from which ions escape slowly. Depolarization increases potassium efflux from the hair cell into that space.
cards.quote: The calyx wraps the type I cell so closely that the cleft between them is very narrow, and ions leave it only slowly.
cards.section: How the cleft can move the calyx

cards.front: In an illustrative calyx, raising cleft potassium shifts E_K from about −80 to −52 mV. With other conductances fixed, what happens to calyx voltage and why?
cards.back: It tends to depolarize. A more positive potassium reversal potential shifts the conductance-weighted balance toward a more positive voltage.
cards.quote: Raising cleft potassium moves E_K toward positive, so, with the other conductances fixed, the weighted average moves up and the calyx tends to depolarize.
cards.section: How the cleft can move the calyx

cards.front: For the calyx inner membrane, potassium current is g_K × (V_calyx − V_cleft − E_K), with outward positive. Holding the other terms fixed, what happens immediately when V_cleft becomes more positive?
cards.back: Outward-positive potassium current decreases: less potassium leaves the calyx, or some enters. The reduced outward current tends to depolarize the calyx.
cards.quote: a more positive cleft, like a higher E_K, shrinks the driving force: less potassium leaves the calyx there, or some enters.
cards.section: How the cleft can move the calyx

cards.front: Why can a single conductance-weighted average of reversal potentials not give the absolute calyx voltage?
cards.back: That rule assumes one common outside voltage. The calyx inner face sees the cleft and its outer face the bath, so it only gives directional guidance here.
cards.quote: The calyx breaks the common-outside condition, because its inner face sees the cleft and its outer face the bath
cards.section: How the cleft can move the calyx

cards.front: A type I hair cell depolarizes and its calyx follows. Why does recording calyx voltage alone fail to distinguish cleft-potassium accumulation from a cleft-potential change?
cards.back: Both mechanisms reduce outward potassium driving force and can depolarize the calyx. Combining the two cleft rules means voltage alone cannot separate them; direct cleft potassium and potential measurements would test their contributions.
cards.quote: The second consequence needs only a subtraction.
cards.section: How the cleft can move the calyx

cards.front: Fast bidirectional coupling was recorded in turtle hair-cell–calyx pairs, while an adult-rat-geometry model predicted cleft potential changing before potassium accumulated. Does this establish that sequence in mature mammals?
cards.back: No. The evidence rule is to separate species-specific recordings from model outputs. Turtle coupling is measured, but the proposed mammalian cleft sequence remains a prediction requiring direct measurement.
cards.quote: These are turtle recordings, not mammalian latencies.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, three animals

cards.front: The internal copy of a motor command used to predict neck feedback is called an {{c1::efference copy}}.
cards.back: It can be compared with actual neck proprioception.
cards.quote: It has an internal copy of the motor command sent to the neck muscles, called an efference copy
cards.section: Passing on the surprise

cards.front: Why must cancellation of self-generated head-motion responses in the tested monkey vestibular-only neurons occur centrally?
cards.back: Canal afferents still respond during both active and passive motion. The reduced active response therefore arises after the peripheral signal reaches the brain.
cards.quote: So any cancellation of your own movement must happen centrally.
cards.section: Passing on the surprise

cards.front: A macaque makes a voluntary head turn, but imposed neck torque makes proprioceptive feedback differ from the motor command’s prediction. What happens to the tested vestibular-only neurons’ responses, and why?
cards.back: Responses become strong rather than largely cancelled. In the neurons tested, cancellation requires actual neck feedback to match predicted feedback; a motor command alone is insufficient.
cards.quote: Neither the motor command nor neck feedback alone was enough.
cards.section: Passing on the surprise

cards.front: In a toy head-motion response, a passive turn peaking at 20 degrees/s evokes 40 spikes/s of modulation; an equally large active turn evokes 4 spikes/s. Calculate both sensitivities and cancellation, defined as 1 − active/passive sensitivity.
cards.back: Passive sensitivity = 40/20 = 2.0 (spikes/s)/(degree/s). Active sensitivity = 4/20 = 0.2 in the same units. Cancellation = 1 − 0.2/2.0 = 0.90 = 90%.
cards.quote: An active turn of the same size evokes 4 spikes per second, so sensitivity is 0.2
cards.section: Passing on the surprise

cards.front: A macaque adapts to turning its head against resistance. What should happen to rostral fastigial vestibular sensitivity when the load is unexpectedly removed, and why?
cards.back: Sensitivity should rise again, as on catch trials. The learned prediction no longer matches feedback when the load unexpectedly disappears.
cards.quote: On catch trials, when the load was unexpectedly removed, sensitivity rose again.
cards.section: Keeping the prediction calibrated

cards.front: A candidate neural prediction-error signal decreases while behaviour adapts to a new load and rebounds on surprise load removal. What further experiment would test whether the signal causes adaptation?
cards.back: Perturb the candidate signal while keeping load and sensory conditions comparable, and measure adaptation against a control. This follows the rule that matched neural and behavioural changes in recordings alone cannot establish causation.
cards.quote: recordings alone cannot show that these neurons cause the learning.
cards.section: Keeping the prediction calibrated

cards.front: What motion signal did the described vestibular implant supply, and what natural vestibular coding did it omit?
cards.back: It stimulated three canal-nerve branches to encode rotation, without natural regular/irregular coding or otolith signals for linear acceleration and tilt.
cards.quote: it encodes no otolith signal for linear acceleration or tilt.
cards.section: Rebuilding the signal: a vestibular implant

cards.front: An eight-person vestibular implant cohort showed some balance improvements and lower dizziness handicap, alongside hearing loss in most implanted ears. What conclusion is justified?
cards.back: The cohort supports feasibility and a benefit–hearing-cost trade-off. Its small single-arm design does not establish population efficacy; the unadjusted balance comparisons also need caution.
cards.quote: establishes feasibility and a trade-off, not population efficacy.
cards.section: Rebuilding the signal: a vestibular implant

cards.front: Design a test of whether non-quantal transmission speeds calyx-bearing irregular afferents. What controls and result would make the conclusion specific to the synapse?
cards.back: Selectively remove non-quantal transmission; compare rapid-stimulus latency and timing before and after. Verify intact quantal release and hair-cell receptor potentials. Use dye-identified bouton-only controls and compare calyx-bearing regular fibres. Unchanged latency and timing in irregular calyx-bearing fibres would count against the hypothesis.
cards.quote: Check quantal release by capacitance and record the hair cell's receptor potential, so that any change can be pinned on the synapse.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Selective silencing of irregular afferents left the VOR largely unchanged during the head rotations tested in squirrel monkeys. What can be inferred about the regular channel?
cards.back: It can support the VOR for those stimuli. The result does not establish that irregular afferents are unnecessary for every stimulus or reflex.
cards.quote: the regular channel can carry the VOR, at least for those stimuli.
cards.section: Does the vestibulo-ocular reflex need the fast channel?

cards.front: A made-up type II hair-cell recording has a sustained capacitance rise of 74 fF. Assuming 37 aF per vesicle, estimate vesicle release and the count for tenfold smaller exocytosis.
cards.back: 74 fF = 74,000 aF; 74,000/37 = 2,000 vesicles. Tenfold smaller exocytosis gives 7.4 fF = 7,400 aF, or 200 vesicles. These are estimates under the conversion assumption.
cards.quote: They converted capacitance to vesicle number with 37 aF per vesicle.
cards.section: Counting vesicles from capacitance

cards.front: Why should a large transient capacitance change in type I vestibular hair cells not automatically be counted as vesicle release?
cards.back: It can arise from potassium-conductance gating rather than fusion. Only the sustained component counts as release in the described preparation.
cards.quote: so only the sustained component counts as release.
cards.section: Counting vesicles from capacitance

cards.front: Treat the measured turtle mean coupling, 522 pS, as a simple transfer conductance. With the calyx voltage held fixed, what current-change magnitude follows an assumed 10 mV hair-cell voltage change?
cards.back: |ΔI| = G|ΔV| = (522 × 10⁻¹² S)(10 × 10⁻³ V) = 5.22 × 10⁻¹² A ≈ 5.2 pA. The voltage change is assumed; the mean coupling does not describe every pair.
cards.quote: Treating the coupling as a simple transfer conductance, the calyx current changes by 522 pS x 10 mV = 5.2 pA.
cards.section: The three preparations, in numbers

cards.front: Why do time constants of 34 ± 7 trials for head velocity and 24 ± 8 trials for neuronal sensitivity not show that neural learning started first?
cards.back: Time constants describe the rate of change, not its onset. The reported constants also did not differ significantly.
cards.quote: Time constants measure rate, not onset, so they cannot say whether neurons or behaviour changed first.
cards.section: Learning rates in the load experiment

cards.front: In the monkey floccular recordings, why was a climbing-fibre error signal not sufficient evidence that Purkinje-cell plasticity occurred on the next trial?
cards.back: Climbing fibres responded during both gain-increase and gain-decrease training, but only during gain-increase training did activity predict reduced Purkinje output on the next trial.
cards.quote: a climbing-fibre error signal does not always trigger plasticity.
cards.section: A different circuit: how the VOR's gain is taught

cards.front: A model predicts that the same climbing-fibre activation must always increase VOR gain, regardless of local inhibition. How do the described interneuron experiments challenge it?
cards.back: In awake mice, co-activation with molecular-layer interneurons could yield a gain decrease instead. Combining the gating and inhibition findings shows that the teaching signal’s effect depends on circuit state, not just climbing-fibre activation.
cards.quote: added that inhibition shapes the teaching signal.
cards.section: A different circuit: how the VOR's gain is taught

cards.front: Dizziness Handicap Inventory group medians are 79 before implantation and 19 afterward. Their difference is compared with a reported median paired improvement of 50 points. Calculate the group-median difference and explain why it need not equal the paired median.
cards.back: 79 − 19 = 60 points. The paired median is computed by subtracting within each participant first, then taking the median. Medians are nonlinear, so 60 and the reported 50 answer different questions.
cards.quote: A median is not a linear summary, so the median of paired changes can differ from the difference of group medians
cards.section: Reading the implant cohort

cards.front: In an implant study, baseline and six-month scores are compared, then motion-modulated and constant stimulation are compared blindly in randomized order on the same day. What causal question does the second comparison address?
cards.back: It tests an immediate effect of motion-modulated stimulation while holding surgery and elapsed time fixed. By the confounding rule, it cannot isolate long-term surgical effects or months of adaptation from the baseline comparison.
cards.quote: it holds the surgery and the elapsed time fixed and addresses expectancy and spontaneous recovery
cards.section: Reading the implant cohort
